sections.title: Prerequisites & Intuition (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Briefly review the standard basis vectors (i, j, k) in 3D space. Introduce the concept that a transformation is defined by where these three basis vectors land after the movement.
sections.example: Imagine a 3D unit cube. If we stretch it, the basis vectors (1,0,0), (0,1,0), and (0,0,1) change their positions, dictating the new shape of the entire space.

sections.title: The Transformation Matrix (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain that a 3x3 matrix represents a linear transformation. Each column represents the destination vector for the original i, j, and k basis vectors respectively. Emphasize that 'linearity' means grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced.
sections.example: Representing a shear: If i moves to (1, 0, 0), j moves to (1, 1, 0), and k moves to (0, 0, 1), the matrix columns are [1,0,0]^T, [1,1,0]^T, and [0,0,1]^T.

sections.title: Visualizing Rotations and Scaling (2:00-3:30)
sections.content: Visual exploration of specific transformations. Scaling changes the length of the basis vectors (diagonal elements), while rotation matrices involve trigonometric functions. Animation will show the cube rotating around the z-axis.
sections.example: A 3D character (a robotic bird) in a game engine. Scaling the bird by [2, 0.5, 1] makes it look wider and flatter, changing its bounding box dimensions.

sections.title: Determinants and Composition (3:30-4:30)
sections.content: Introduce the determinant as the 'volume scaling factor' of the transformation. Explain that multiple transformations are computed via matrix multiplication (applying transformations in sequence).
sections.example: If you rotate a 3D model of a dragon and then scale it, the order matters (non-commutative). The volume of the dragon after transformation is the original volume multiplied by the determinant of the matrix.

sections.title: Summary & Real-world Application (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Recap: Linear transformations map space to space. Link back to computer graphics (rendering 3D characters in 2D screens) and physics simulations.
sections.example: In a movie production, an animator uses these matrices to make a 3D alien character 'squash and stretch' realistically as it lands on the ground.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites & Intuition (0:00-0:45)
lecture_lines: Where they land defines the new space.
animations: Show a 3D grid with the unit cube at the origin. Highlight basis vectors i (1,0,0), j (0,1,0), k (0,0,1) in #FF0000, #00FF00, #0000FF.
Stretch the cube along the x-axis, observing i change position.
Stretch the cube along the y-axis, observing j change position.
Stretch the cube along the z-axis, observing k change position.
Overlay the final basis vector positions to illustrate space deformation.

storyboard.title: The Transformation Matrix (0:45-2:00)
lecture_lines: Columns show destinations of basis vectors.
Grid lines remain parallel and uniform.
animations: Display a 3x3 matrix outline with placeholders for basis vectors.
Animate basis vector i moving to the first column position.
Animate basis vector j moving to the second column position.
Animate basis vector k moving to the third column position.
Demonstrate the transformation of a grid, showing lines stay parallel.

storyboard.title: Visualizing Rotations and Scaling (2:00-3:30)
animations: Show a 3D wireframe cube at the origin.
Apply a scaling transformation to show the cube stretching.
Highlight diagonal elements of the scaling matrix in #FFFF00.
Rotate the cube 45 degrees around the z-axis.
Simultaneously display rotation and scaling effect on the cube.

storyboard.title: Determinants and Composition (3:30-4:30)
animations: Represent the object as a unit cube with volume 1.0.
Apply a transformation, show the new volume scaling to det(M).
Display two transformation matrices A and B next to each other.
Perform matrix multiplication A * B to show the composition.
Show that multiplying B * A yields a different result.

storyboard.title: Summary & Real-world Application (4:30-5:00)
animations: Display a summarized 3D character (robotic bird).
Animate the 'squash and stretch' effect using a transformation matrix.
Conclude by showing the 3D model projecting onto a 2D screen.
